We hypothesize that pattern separation (PS) underlies frequency\u2010dependent MD performance. We aim to study, in a computational model of the hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG), the network and cellular mechanisms governing this putative \u201cU\u201d\u2010shaped PS relationship. We implemented a biophysical model of the DG that produces the hypothesized \u201cU\u201d\u2010shaped input frequency\u2013PS relationship, and its associated oscillatory electrophysiological signatures. We subsequently evaluated the network's PS ability using an adapted spatiotemporal task. We undertook systematic lesion studies to identify the network\u2010level mechanisms driving the \u201cU\u201d\u2010shaped input frequency\u2010PS relationship. A minimal circuit of a single granule cell (GC) stimulated with oscillatory inputs was also used to study potential cellular\u2010level mechanisms. Lesioning synapses onto GCs did not impact the \u201cU\u201d\u2010shaped input frequency\u2013PS relationship. Furthermore, GC inhibition limits PS performance for fast frequency inputs, while enhancing PS for slow frequency inputs. GC interspike interval was found to be input frequency dependent in a \u201cU\u201d\u2010shaped fashion, paralleling frequency\u2010dependent PS observed at the network level. Additionally, GCs showed an attenuated firing response for fast frequency inputs. We conclude that independent of network\u2010level inhibition, GCs may intrinsically be capable of producing a \u201cU\u201d\u2010shaped input frequency\u2010PS relationship. GCs may preferentially decorrelate slow and fast inputs via spike timing reorganization and high frequency filtering.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.1002\/hipo.23585","type":"journal-article","created":{"date-parts":[[2023,11,11]],"date-time":"2023-11-11T03:56:12Z","timestamp":1699674972000},"page":"14-28","update-policy":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.1002\/crossmark_policy","source":"Crossref","is-referenced-by-count":7,"title":["Granule
